background: Finished a B.Com two months ago and has only ever used Excel. Comfortable with formulas and pivot tables but has never written a line of code. Applying to analyst roles and keeps being rejected for lacking SQL and Python.
goal: I want to become a data analyst and be employable in about six months.
rationale: SQL first because it is the fastest route to something an employer tests for and needs no programming background. Python before NumPy and pandas because both assume it. Visualisation only after pandas, since the charting course works on DataFrames. The dashboard project is last as it consolidates SQL and visualisation together.

background: Has a strong statistics background from his economics masters and did regressions in Stata, but has never programmed outside of it. Understands distributions and hypothesis testing well. Wants to move from policy research into a data role.
goal: I already know statistics but I cannot code. I want to move into data science.
rationale: He does not need the statistics courses, so those are skipped entirely — this is the case where recommending Khan Academy statistics would be a wasted month. A practical Python course suits someone impatient to apply existing knowledge. Then the standard data stack, then feature engineering and modelling, which his statistics background makes fast.

background: Second-year CS student who has done a semester of Python and used pandas for a class project. Comfortable with loops, functions and DataFrames. Has never done machine learning and finds the maths intimidating.
goal: I want to learn machine learning properly, not just call fit and predict.
rationale: She already has the Python and pandas layer, so starting there would waste her time. Statistics comes first because she named the maths as her weak point and inferential statistics underpins model evaluation. EDA and feature engineering before modelling, then the crash course and model selection for the depth she asked for.

background: Works in supply-chain operations and pulls the same numbers into Excel every week. His manager asked him to build a proper dashboard. No programming background, and he can only study early mornings before work.
goal: I need to build a dashboard for my team at work.
rationale: He already writes basic queries, so he starts at joins rather than SELECT. Everything here is the minimum to reach a working dashboard — no statistics, no machine learning, because his goal is narrow and his hours are scarce. The dashboard project comes last and doubles as the thing his manager asked for.

background: Final-year mechanical engineering student who has decided he wants to build websites instead. Has written a little C for coursework but nothing for the web. Motivated and has a free summer.
goal: I want to become a front-end developer and build real websites.
rationale: HTML then CSS then JavaScript is the standard order and each genuinely assumes the last. Layout before React so he can style what he builds. Modern JavaScript modules before React because React assumes them. Hooks and state after the React fundamentals, and accessibility near the end once he has markup worth making accessible.
